title: Why Time-Out Must Be Taught
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that time-out (or whatever a teacher renames it) only works if it is taught with exhaustive, explicit detail covering seven specific elements, from what the consequence means to the exact conditions for re-entry to class. He explains three reasons this thoroughness matters: it minimizes classroom disruption because sending a student to time-out becomes a near-silent, practiced routine; it eliminates debate because students who fully understand the rules have no grounds to argue when caught; and it ensures effectiveness because students who truly know the plan feel the consequence coming and internalize responsibility rather than resenting it. He contrasts this thorough teaching with what most teachers actually do, which he says leaves students refusing time-out, crying, or complaining to parents about being picked on. The piece closes with a call to teach time-out at this level of detail either at the start of the year or, failing that, immediately.
points: Time-out must be explicitly taught across seven specific components, from its meaning to the exact conditions for leaving it, not just announced as a consequence.
A well-taught time-out routine should be nearly unnoticeable to the rest of the class — a quick word or signal, then straight back to teaching.
When students fully understand where the line is and know they'll be held accountable 100 percent of the time, they stop arguing because arguing is pointless.
Teachers who skip the thorough teaching of time-out are the ones who end up with students refusing it, crying in it, or complaining to parents about being picked on.
Test students' understanding of the time-out process and make them prove they 'got it' before ever putting it into practice.
quotes: But what is important, critically, is that it must be taught. It must be explained in detail, modeled explicitly, and practiced until your students know every step of the time-out process.
Done right, sending a student to time-out should be seamless and virtually unnoticeable to the rest of the class. A quick word or signal from you and then you’re immediately back to teaching.
When students know where the line is that when crossed triggers a consequence, and they’re held accountable 100 percent of the time, then there is no reason to argue.
They feel it like a freedom-loving dog with a shock collar easing over an underground fence. They expect your promised response, which comes as predictable as light after a flipped switch.

However, most teachers don’t teach it to the reaches of thoroughness it requires. And yet they wonder why they have students refusing time-out, crying in time-out, and complaining to their parents that their mean teacher is picking on them.
You must teach time-out in excruciating detail. You must test your students’ understanding and make them prove they “got it” before putting it into practice.
